title: Market Rotation Rewards Diversification
summary: Market leadership is shifting. LPL Research explores concentration risk, improving market breadth, and how diversification can help navigate volatility.

# Market Rotation Rewards Diversification


[John Lohse](https://www.lpl.com/research/research-team/john-lohse.html) | Portfolio Strategist, Model Portfolio Management


Last Updated: November 19, 2026


## When Market Leadership Shifts, Diversification Matters


Periods of market turbulence often provide a useful reminder that what leads the market on the way up may not offer the same protection when conditions become more challenging. After an extended period in which a relatively narrow group of large technology companies drove a significant portion of broad market returns, recent performance has shown signs of a meaningful rotation in market leadership. As we hit the halfway mark of Q4, we’re going to check in on some market drivers and portfolio construction ideas amid this turbulent environment.


In our view, the long-term AI story remains intact and will continue to fuel economic growth, but shifting market leadership reinforces the benefits of diversification. Within tactically oriented model portfolios, we remain overweight equities but have spread that excess exposure to high-quality and value-style domestic large cap stocks. Quality is an important component of this approach. Companies with durable earnings, healthy balance sheets, consistent cash flow generation, and disciplined management teams may be better positioned to navigate changing economic and market conditions. A quality tilt can also help investors maintain equity exposure without taking unnecessary balance sheet, earnings, or idiosyncratic risk. Market concentration is your friend until it isn’t. Nor does it pay you for taking on idiosyncratic risk. The “Concentration Risk” chart highlights the top five and bottom five quarter-to-date (QTD) return drivers of the Bloomberg 500 Index through November 16. From the start of Q4 through November 16, the index’s price dropped 3.2%. 81% of that decline is attributable to a single stock within that roughly 500-name index, NVIDIA (NVDA). We won’t rehash the recent events here but will point out the need to remain aware of concentrated index risk.

## A Market Rotation Beneath the Surface


Halfway through the quarter, the performance gap between the equal-weighted and capitalization-weighted versions of the S&P 500 provides evidence of broadening market leadership. During periods when a small number of mega-cap companies dominate returns, the capitalization-weighted index tends to outperform. By contrast, relative strength in the equal- weighted index generally indicates that the average stock is performing better and market participation is expanding. Through the first 33 trading days of the quarter (through November 16), the S&P 500 Equal Weight Index experienced a positive 5.1% price return, while the market-cap weighted S&P 500 Index shed 3.1%. That positive 8.2% price delta is the second- largest 33-day rolling difference over the past 10 years. That lookback covers nearly 2,500 trading days and has only seen a higher positive divergence one time, in June 2020. The “Equal Weight Dominance” chart highlights this extreme divergence.


### Equal Weight Dominance


Broader participation can be a constructive signal for the overall health of the equity market. It may also create a more favorable environment for active management, factor diversification, and exposure to value-oriented companies that have not participated as fully in the market’s recent advance. Tactically, our model portfolios are capturing elements of this environment as our Tactical Asset Allocation (TAA) guidance favors large cap value equities over large cap growth on a relative basis. The Russell 1000 Value Index’s price has increased 4.9% over that same time period, while the Russell 1000 Growth Index’s price has lost 11%. In concert with the quality bias mentioned above, we’ve seen the benefits of capitalizing on shorter-term market dislocations through a well-informed asset allocation.


## Investor Takeaway


Market turbulence often exposes the risks hidden by periods of strong performance. Concentrated portfolios can perform exceptionally well when leadership is narrow and persistent, but they also become more vulnerable when sentiment changes or market leadership rotates. Investors do not need to predict every rotation in advance if their portfolios are built to participate in more than one possible outcome. In the current environment, maintaining a modest equity overweight, emphasizing quality, balancing growth exposure with a value tilt, and diversifying across market themes may provide a more durable path through turbulence. The goal is not to avoid volatility altogether; it is to construct allocations and portfolios capable of navigating it.
